He may recognize the political pressure to address immigration while remaining cautious about losing support from his most loyal voters. But here's where things get interesting: Congress doesn't necessarily need Trump's approval to pass immigration reform. If enough Republicans join Democrats in supporting legislation, Congress could potentially override a presidential veto with a two-thirds majority in both chambers. That raises an important question about the future of immigration policy. Could moderate Republicans and Democrats find enough common ground to pass meaningful immigration reform, even without the president's support? The possibility of bipartisan cooperation has existed before. Whether lawmakers are willing to pursue it again remains to be seen.
